description: Delivered in October 2012 with sponsorship from the Legacy Trust, after which the main hangar was named the Legacy Jet Centre. Maintained in full running and taxi order.

description: Fuselage only. Imported as a spares source for the airworthy New Zealand Catalina, then dumped at Ardmore as a stripped shell and restored to show a wartime interior. Marked 204.
Restored from a wreck recovered in the Pacific islands and painted in the colours of No. 112 Squadron RAF, Western Desert. Marked GA-K.
Elementary trainer biplane.
Second Devon in the collection.
Ex-RNZAF NZ1802, a six-seat VIP Devon recovered from a paddock in South Auckland and restored for museum display.
Ex-Swiss Air Force J-1799, brought to New Zealand by John Luft and donated to the museum after a crash at the Masterton airshow.
Named Matapouri; the sole survivor of the four Herons bought by the National Airways Corporation. Maintained with the two outer engines in running order.
Ex-RAF WA374, RNZAF instructional airframe INST202. Previously a fuselage-only display at RNZAF Base Ohakea; reported in July 2024 as being prepared for mounting on a plinth at Classic Flyers.
Second Vampire at Classic Flyers; listed by Wikipedia as under restoration here.
BuNo 157904, the first RNZAF Skyhawk. Acquired by public subscription in Tauranga after the 2001 disbandment of the air combat force. Kept in the hangar because it is difficult to move.
American two-seat light aircraft.
Full-scale replica marked DK791/4C; formerly at MOTAT and donated to Classic Flyers.
Airframe number 124 built by Air Parts, marked to represent the prototype Fletcher ZK-BDS. Moved out of the hangar in 2024 and now displayed outside.
Ex-Singapore Hunter, marked 517.
Wears the RNZAF yellow and black scheme and the serial NZ1935; used for adventure flights.
French-built Messerschmitt Bf 108 derivative.
Painted to represent the aircraft of Korean War ace Captain Joseph McConnell; marked FU-910.
Ex-RNZAF NZ1066, owned by a syndicate of pilots and used for adventure flights. aviationmuseum.eu instead lists two Classic Flyers Harvards, ZK-ENC (NZ1091) and ZK-ENJ (NZ1098).

Single-seat aerobatic biplane.
British club sailplane of 1957.

Full-scale fibreglass and wood replica located in Australia, shipped to New Zealand and reassembled; incorporates some genuine Spitfire components and is fitted with a Vokes desert filter. Carries the code CRC for Australian ace Clive Caldwell; aviationmuseum.eu records the markings as JK715/SN-A.
Flew with No. 30 Squadron RNZAF and was one of the last three Avengers in RNZAF service, sold 23 September 1959. Stored at various locations before arriving at Classic Flyers in 2017.
Reputed to be New Zealand's first home-built glider, built in 1961 to Stan Hall's 1956 design and rescued from destruction for display.
Single-seat wooden sailplane built in 1965; crashed in 2007 and rebuilt by volunteers led by former owner Ann Johnson, who set New Zealand women's records in it including a height of 28000 ft.
Foot-launched ultralight glider built locally from Dieter Reich's 1993 plans; left un-skinned to show the structure. Uses tennis balls as a landing-skid shock damper.
Fuselage section from a film set, delivered in pieces in 2019-2020 and assembled by museum volunteers as a walk-through exhibit along the back wall.
Ex-MOTAT Pearse replica, displayed indoors from 2024 alongside a Pearse experimental test airframe.
Experimental airframe built to test the feasibility of Richard Pearse's original design; displayed alongside the ex-MOTAT replica.
Canadian ultralight.
Single-seat homebuilt.
Australian-built Airtourer, marked 60.
